lines: A tiny array of bits, nowhere near as large as the actual set it's standing in for.
It can still answer one real question about something it has never actually stored anywhere.
Could this possibly belong to the set at all.
Worth reasoning through before settling on an answer.
Something was genuinely added earlier, and now it's being checked against that same tiny array again.
Could that check ever come back saying it's absent, even though it was truly added before?
answer: No, never — a check like that always comes back saying the thing is present.
Whatever got flipped on when something was added stays flipped on forever afterward.
Checking that same thing again later always finds every one of those same spots still on, so a genuine member can never slip through as missing.

lines: Here's exactly where that guarantee actually comes from.
Adding something flips on a handful of spots in the array, chosen by how that thing hashes.
Checking it later looks at those exact same spots — if they were turned on going in, they're still on coming back out.
How large that array needs to be isn't arbitrary at all.
Setting aside fewer spots per item leaves things more crowded, and crowding is exactly what causes a false alarm.
Choosing a target rate for those false alarms directly decides how much room, and how many spots per item, the whole structure actually needs.
steps.takeaway: Choosing a target false-alarm rate directly decides how much room a filter needs.

lines: Here's that sizing choice checked against something built and measured for real.
A real array, sized exactly that way, gets checked against a huge batch of things that were genuinely never added to it.
How often it actually gets fooled tracks what that sizing choice predicted, closely.
steps.takeaway: A real filter's measured false-alarm rate tracks its own sizing choice closely.

lines: Here's one real thing this tiny array can never do on its own.
Taking back just one single thing that was added would mean starting the entire array over from scratch, in the structure's own original description.
A close cousin structure adds a genuine way around that: it keeps an actual fingerprint for each item, which it can simply remove directly.
steps.takeaway: That close cousin adds a genuine way to remove one item, by keeping a removable fingerprint.

lines: Two further cousins trade something else entirely for an even smaller footprint.
Both need every single item known completely up front, and neither one can ever be changed again once it's finished being built.

What they get back for that is using noticeably less room per item than the structures before them — a real, widely used storage engine's own documentation names that exact trade for the one it actually ships.
steps.takeaway: Both cousins trade a one-time, costlier build for using noticeably less room per item.

lines: Pulling the whole topic back together.
Something genuinely added can never come back looking absent. Choosing a target false-alarm rate decides how much room gets used, and a real build tracks that choice closely.
One cousin adds a genuine way to remove a single item. Two further cousins trade a costlier, one-time build for using noticeably less room per item.
One closing scenario, worth reasoning through before the explanation lands.
A system already keeps one of these tiny arrays per stored file, skipping over any file that plainly can't hold what's being looked for, before ever touching the disk.
A teammate wants to swap that array for the cousin that can remove single items directly. What would that cousin actually add here, and does this system even need it?
answer: Nothing much, in this particular case — the system doesn't need that swap at all.
That cousin's real advantage is removing one single item directly, without starting over.
This system only ever drops one of these arrays by dropping the entire file it belongs to, so there's nothing here for that extra ability to actually buy.
